The template from the template extractor lacks the colors entry needed to build the palette.
Empty projects make some charts crash.
No tests are visible for this file.

terms.meaning: A charting library that draws interactive charts in a web page.
A bar chart that shows when each task starts and ends on a timeline.
A smaller chart placed inside a larger figure with others.
A color written as a code such as a hash followed by six characters.
A table of rows and columns used for data analysis.
Placing nodes evenly around a circle, which shows order but not distance.

depends_on: data_models (ProjectStructure, Workstream, Module, Activity, DependencyGraph, OptimizationResult)

sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Imports of charting and data tools
sections.what: Loads the charting, table, math, and project data tools that this module uses.
sections.why: Likely reason: charts are drawn with Plotly, and the template helper is imported to pick colors.
sections.watch_out: Imports a function named extract_proposal_template from template_extractor, which the shown template file does not define, so this import fails.

sections.name: ProjectVisualizer (part 1)
sections.title: Setting up the chart builder
sections.what: Stores the project and a template, then builds the palette of workstream colors from that template.
sections.why: Likely reason: matches the charts to the example proposal's colors, as the docstring says.
sections.watch_out: Expects a colors entry holding chart colors, which the template extractor does not produce.

sections.name: ProjectVisualizer: create_gantt_chart
sections.title: Building the timeline data
sections.what: Prepares the task rows for the main timeline chart, with one row per workstream and optionally one per module.
sections.why: Likely reason: a timeline chart needs a flat list of tasks with start and end weeks.
sections.watch_out: Colors are picked by position, so an optimized list with a different count than the palette can run out of colors.

sections.name: ProjectVisualizer (part 3)
sections.title: Drawing the timeline bars
sections.what: Adds one bar per task with hover details, then sets the week range, height, and white background.
sections.why: Likely reason: hover text shows exact start and end weeks so the reader can check dates.
sections.watch_out: An empty project makes the maximum-week calculation fail.

sections.name: ProjectVisualizer: create_timeline_comparison
sections.title: Original versus optimized timeline
sections.what: Draws two stacked timelines, the original and the optimized one, with a heading that states the weeks saved.
sections.why: Likely reason: shows the effect of optimization at a glance.
sections.watch_out: The heading reads weeks saved from the result object, so a missing result stops the chart.

sections.name: ProjectVisualizer (part 5)
sections.title: Comparison axes and dependency node setup
sections.what: Gives both comparison panels the same week range and sets the heading style. It also starts the dependency network by listing each workstream as a node in start-week order.
sections.why: Likely reason: a shared range makes the two panels comparable, and ordering by start week keeps the layout close to the timeline.
sections.watch_out: The empty-data check depends on the dependencies object being falsy, which a data object usually is not, so the empty message may never appear.

sections.name: ProjectVisualizer (part 6)
sections.title: Placing dependency nodes on a circle
sections.what: Places each workstream on a circle, draws a line from each dependency to the workstream that needs it, and adds the labels.
sections.why: Likely reason: a circle is a simple layout that needs no extra graph library.
sections.watch_out: Positions show order only, not real timing, and dependencies that point to unknown IDs are skipped without a message.

sections.name: ProjectVisualizer (part 7)
sections.title: Finishing the network and listing breakdown rows
sections.what: Sets the network title, hides the axes, and returns the figure. The breakdown builder then lists each module and its activities as rows.
sections.why: Likely reason: a plain figure keeps the network easy to read.
sections.watch_out: Activity start weeks add up one after another inside each module, so activities are assumed to run in sequence even if they overlap.

sections.name: ProjectVisualizer (part 8)
sections.title: Drawing module and activity bars
sections.what: Draws module bars in blue and activity bars in a lighter grey, then sets the title and height.
sections.why: Likely reason: color and tone separate the main items from their parts.
sections.watch_out: Colors are fixed in this function rather than taken from the template, so this view will not match the proposal's style.

sections.name: ProjectVisualizer: create_resource_allocation_chart
sections.title: Counting busy workstreams each week
sections.what: Counts how many workstreams are active in each week and draws the counts as a colored bar chart.
sections.why: Likely reason: shows where the workload peaks across the timeline.
sections.watch_out: Finding the last week fails on a project with no workstreams.

sections.name: ProjectVisualizer: create_summary_dashboard
sections.title: Building the four-panel dashboard
sections.what: Creates a four-panel layout and fills the first two panels: workstream durations as bars and module counts as a pie chart.
sections.why: Likely reason: one page gives the owner a quick overview of the project.

sections.name: ProjectVisualizer (part 11)
sections.title: Timeline and activity panels of dashboard
sections.what: Adds a timeline line for each workstream and an activity-count bar chart, then labels all the axes.
sections.why: Likely reason: the two panels give one schedule view and one count view.
sections.watch_out: Axis labels follow the list order, so reordering the workstreams without updating the labels would mislabel them.

sections.name: ProjectVisualizer (part 12)
sections.title: Dashboard title and blank placeholder chart
sections.what: Sets the dashboard title and size, adding the weeks saved when a result is given. It also provides a blank chart with a short message for when there is nothing to show.
sections.why: Likely reason: the blank chart avoids a crash when a chart has no data.
sections.watch_out: The blank chart is used only by the network and breakdown views, so other charts with no data may still fail.

sections.name: ProjectVisualizer: export_all_charts
sections.title: Exporting all charts to files
sections.what: Creates the output folder, builds four main charts, saves each as an HTML file, prints a count, and returns the file paths.
sections.why: Likely reason: HTML files open in any web browser and can be shared without Python.
sections.watch_out: The docstring promises PNG images, but only HTML files are written.

summary: Builds interactive Plotly charts of the project timeline, dependencies, resource load, and a summary dashboard, and saves four of them as HTML files.
purpose: Let the owner see the project plan visually and check it before use.
why: The docstring says the charts use colors taken from an example proposal so they match its look. The reason for the other chart choices is not stated in the code.
how: The visualizer stores the project and a template, and builds a color palette from the template. Each chart method builds its own Plotly figure. The export method creates the output folder, builds four charts, and writes each to an HTML file.
inputs: A ProjectStructure object, an optional template dictionary, optional optimized workstream lists, an OptimizationResult, and an output folder.
outputs: Plotly figure objects that the app can show, four HTML files in output/visualizations, and a dictionary of their file paths.
risks: The module imports a function named extract_proposal_template from template_extractor, which that file does not define, so the import fails. The palette expects a colors entry in the template, which the template extractor does not produce. An empty project crashes the Gantt and resource charts. Palette colors are chosen by position, so an optimized list of a different length can run out of colors. The export docstring promises PNG images, but only HTML is written. The dependency network uses a circle layout rather than a true graph layout.
debug: First look at the import error, since it stops the whole module. Next check the template dictionary for a colors key. For a maximum-of-empty error, confirm the project has workstreams. For color errors, compare the length of the optimized list with the original. To view results, open the HTML files in a browser.
